muni.unknown: We do not know postcode area {pc}. Check the digits. The route below still applies.

route.note: Ages and school years are typical. Children can start, repeat or switch at different times, and the school decides. Check every date and rule with the school and your municipality.

age.note: These are average ages. Children can skip or repeat a year, also in primary school, and the school decides.

pre.title: Before school: choose and register
what: A child may start primary school at age 4, and you can register from age 3. Many schools let a child come for a few settling-in days from age 3 years 10 months, up to 5 in total, but not every school offers them. Compulsory attendance starts on the first day of the month after the fifth birthday.
Public schools are open to every child. A denominational or other "special" school works from a religion or belief. Both kinds can follow methods such as Montessori or Dalton.
todo: Visit two or three schools and read their school guide.
Ask each school how sign-up and any waiting list work.

g12.title: Year groups 1 and 2
what: The first two years of primary school, which has eight year groups. Most children start on their fourth birthday.
todo: Nothing to sign up for.
Ask how the school decides when a child moves on to year group 3. The school decides, together with you.

g35.title: Year groups 3 to 5
what: The school keeps a record of your child's progress. The school advice in year group 8 is the school's judgement of that whole record.
todo: Ask for a talk once a year, and ask early if you are worried.
If the school suggests repeating a year, ask for the reasons in writing (see Questions).

g67.title: Year groups 6 and 7
what: Many schools start talking with parents about a likely secondary level around now. The formal advice is only given in year group 8.
todo: Ask the teacher when your school starts the conversation.
Look at secondary schools and their open days. Dates differ per school.

g8.title: Year group 8: advice, test and sign-up
what: In year group 8 the school gives a school advice (schooladvies) and your child takes an end-of-primary test. The advice can name one level or two, for example havo and vwo. You sign up at a secondary school with the final advice.
g8.whatDated: Dates for school year 2026-27. They are set again every year.
g8.whatUsual: The usual pattern: provisional advice in January, the test from late January into February, final advice in March, and sign-up at the end of March. The exact dates are set each year. For your child this is {label}.
todo: Visit open days and make a short list of schools that offer the advised level.
Ask how your region organises sign-up, and sign up within the sign-up week.
Remember a school may refuse a child only on limited grounds, such as having no places left.

vo1.title: First year of secondary school (brugklas)
what: Year 1 usually lasts one year, sometimes two. Many schools combine at least two levels in one class, for example vmbo-t with havo, or havo with vwo. Some schools are single-level and start in one level directly.
todo: Ask how and when a child can move up or down a level. The school decides.
Ask what extra support the school gives.

vo23.title: Years 2 and 3: choosing a pathway or profile
what: In vmbo, pupils choose a learning pathway (basis, kader, mixed or theoretical) and a sector by the end of year 2. In havo and vwo, pupils choose one of four profiles before the upper years: nature and technology, nature and health, economics and society, or culture and society. Schools usually ask at the end of year 3.
After year 3 of havo or vwo, a recognised pass certificate also gives access to mbo level 2, 3 or 4.
todo: Ask which profiles the school offers and which studies each one opens.
Moving between levels in these years is sometimes possible. The school decides.

fin.title: Exam year and what comes next
what: The final exam year is year 4 in vmbo (age 15 to 16), year 5 in havo (age 16 to 17) and year 6 in vwo (age 17 to 18). Practical education runs to about age 18.
todo: For mbo, apply to the programme by 1 April of the exam year. You can apply later, but then you have no right to admission.
For hbo or wo, check the subjects and application dates of each programme early.

he.title: After secondary school: mbo, hbo or wo
what: mbo (vocational college) has four levels: level 1 takes 1 year, level 2 takes 1 to 2, level 3 takes 2 to 3 and level 4 takes 3 to 4 years. A level 4 diploma gives the right to enter hbo.
hbo (university of applied sciences): a bachelor takes 4 years, and the first year is the first-year certificate (propedeuse). An associate degree takes 2 years. A master takes 1 to 2 years.

wo (research university): a bachelor takes 3 years and a master 1 to 3 years. A PhD takes about 4 years. With a havo diploma, the usual route to wo is an hbo first year, and in most cases the university then decides. An hbo bachelor usually needs a bridging programme (pre-master) before a wo master.
Without the usual diploma, people from age 21 can ask for an admission test (21+ test). Each institution runs its own.
todo: Check the entry rules, dates and any selection of each programme.

newc.when: First, usually for up to about two years
newc.unit: usually up to about two years

young.title: Newcomer class in primary school
young.what: Parents usually choose between a special language class (schakelklas) for children who just arrived, and a regular class with extra Dutch lessons. A temporary newcomer provision can enrol a child for at most 2 years in total.

old.title: Newcomer class in secondary school (ISK)
old.what: A special class at a regular secondary school for recently arrived pupils who speak little or no Dutch. Lessons cover Dutch, maths and citizenship, and prepare pupils for regular secondary or mbo education. Most pupils stay up to about two years, then move to a regular class.

todo: Ask your municipality, a reception location or the nearest school where places exist.
Places can be limited in some cities, so ask early.

path.pro: Practical education (praktijkonderwijs): pupils can usually stay until the end of the school year in which they turn 18, on average about five years. Next: the mbo entry programme (level 1, one year, no earlier diploma needed, from age 16) or a work route that the school arranges with the mbo college.
path.vbk: vmbo basis or kader: a diploma after 4 years. Basis leads to mbo level 2 (1 to 2 years). Kader leads to mbo level 3 (2 to 3 years) or level 4 (3 to 4 years), as the official entry requirements for 3 and 4 are the same. Programmes can add their own conditions, so ask the mbo college. A lower level is usually possible, and moving up later within mbo is possible.
path.vgt: vmbo gl/tl: a diploma after 4 years. Leads to mbo level 3 or 4. Moving to havo year 4 is possible with an extra exam subject or other conditions, and the school decides.
path.havo: havo: a diploma after 5 years. Leads to an hbo bachelor (4 years), an associate degree (2 years), mbo at any level, or vwo (the school decides the year, many use year 5). A havo diploma alone does not give access to wo.
path.vwo: vwo: a diploma after 6 years. Leads to a wo bachelor (3 years), an hbo bachelor or an associate degree. Some studies ask for particular subjects or select applicants.

pre.title: Choose and register at a primary school
pre.text: There is no national deadline. Visit schools and ask each how sign-up and any waiting list work.

early.title: First big step: school advice and secondary sign-up
early.text: Until then there is nothing to sign up for. Keep in touch with the teacher and ask early if you are worried about progress.

vo.title: No national deadline right now
vo.text: Level and profile choices are made by the school. Ask when they are made and what they mean for later studies.

fin.title: Apply to the mbo programme
fin.text: For mbo, apply by 1 April of the exam year to keep the right to admission. For hbo or wo, each programme sets its own dates.

he.title: Check dates and entry rules
he.text: Each programme sets its own application dates and entry rules.

dates.d: The school gives a provisional advice. Ask for a talk and ask what it is based on.
Your child takes the test at school. If the result is higher than the provisional advice, the school adjusts the advice upward, unless it explains why that is not in your child's interest.
The school sets the final advice. Secondary schools admit on this final advice.
Sign up at the secondary school you choose, with the final advice. Many regions allow more than one school, so check how yours works.

amsterdam.title: Amsterdam
amsterdam.text: Amsterdam runs a central lottery and matching procedure (centrale loting en matching) for secondary school. As we understand it, you rank schools that fit the school advice, each pupil gets a lot number, and places are matched using your ranking and the lot number. Do not assume the rules you know from another city apply here. The exact steps, the schools that take part and the dates change each year. Use the official Amsterdam sources and ask your child's school.

advice.title: Where pupils go next: school advice
advice.expl: At the end of group 8, the school gives each child a school advice (schooladvies), the secondary level it recommends. The bar shows the advice given to the school's leavers. It describes the pupils the school has, not how good the school is. Schools with a different intake will show a different mix.

test.title: End-of-primary test (doorstroomtoets)
test.expl: In group 8 every child takes an end-of-primary test. Schools choose from several approved tests, and each test has its own scale. Never compare the score of one test with another. The average is context for the school advice, not a grade for the school.
test.note: Only compare schools that used the same test.

dist.title: How far pupils live
dist.expl: This is the straight-line distance between pupils' homes and the school. A small number means the school is mostly a neighbourhood school. A large number means pupils travel in from further away, which can matter for cycling and for friendships after school.

levels.title: Levels offered
levels.expl: Dutch secondary school has several levels. In vmbo there are four variants: basis and kader (more practical), and gl and tl (more theoretical). Then come havo (5 years) and vwo (6 years). A school can offer one level or several. A school with several levels under one roof makes it easier to move up or down later. The school decides on moving.

pass.explShort: The national exam happens in the last year of each level. Pass rates depend on who the school admits and on how many candidates there are.
pass.expl: In the final year of each level, pupils sit the national exam. The pass rate is the share of candidates who passed. It also depends on which pupils the school admits and, for small groups, on chance. It is not a ranking, and a high rate is not the same as a good fit for your child.

insp.expl: The Dutch Inspectorate of Education visits schools and judges their quality. It mostly publishes a judgement after a visit, and visits are often triggered by concerns. So having a judgement, or not having one, says little by itself. We do not sort, colour or average schools by it.

sbo.title: About special primary schools
sbo.text: A special primary school (sbo) is for children who need more support than a regular school can give. Admission needs a formal decision first. Ask your child's current school or your municipality.

sys.heading: The whole system on one page
sys.intro: Read from top to bottom. Each block is one school year. Every track has its own colour, and higher education has colours of its own, because finishing one school does not move a child on automatically: each change needs a diploma, an application and sometimes selection. No track is ranked above another.
sys.arrowNote: An arrow means a child can move that way. A solid arrow means the diploma normally gives the right to move. A dashed arrow means conditions, selection or a school decision apply. Letters and numbers match the list.
sys.title: The Dutch school system, top to bottom
sys.desc: Primary school of eight year groups leads, after school advice, to practical education, vmbo, havo or vwo. After those come mbo, hbo and wo. Arrows show how children can move between tracks.
sys.adviceLabel: School advice and sign-up, about age 12

xfers.text: After year group 8 (about age 12) the school advice and your sign-up decide the secondary track. The advice can name one level or two, such as havo and vwo.
Early years of secondary school: moving up or down a level is sometimes possible, and the school decides. Dashed because it is not a right.
vmbo gl/tl to havo year 4: possible with an extra exam subject or other conditions that the school sets.
havo diploma to vwo: possible. The school decides which year your child joins, many use year 5.
Practical education to the mbo entry programme (level 1) or to work: the school arranges this with the mbo college.
vmbo diploma to mbo: basis leads to level 2. Kader, mixed or theoretical lead to level 3 or 4, because the official entry requirements for those are the same. A lower level is usually possible.
havo diploma to an hbo bachelor, an associate degree or mbo at any level. It does not give direct access to wo.
vwo diploma to a wo bachelor, or to an hbo bachelor or associate degree. Some studies ask for particular subjects or select.
An mbo level 4 diploma gives the right to enter hbo.
hbo first year (propedeuse) to a wo bachelor: possible in most cases, but the university decides and subject requirements can still apply.
hbo bachelor to a wo master: usually through a bridging programme (pre-master). Length and cost differ per programme, and selection is possible.

sys.xfersExtra: Other arrows without a letter: bachelor to master and master to PhD. Selection is possible at each.

items.q: What does "university" mean here (wo vs hbo)?

blocks.p: Dutch higher education has two kinds. wo is the research university: more theory, and a bachelor takes 3 years. hbo is the university of applied sciences: more practice, and a bachelor takes 4 years. Outside the Netherlands both are often called "university", so check which one a document means.

ul: vwo is the usual route to wo. havo leads to hbo. An mbo level 4 diploma also gives the right to enter hbo.
A havo diploma alone does not give access to wo. After the first hbo year (the propedeuse), wo is possible in most cases, but the university decides and subject requirements can still apply.
People from age 21 without the usual diploma can ask for an admission test (the 21+ test). Each institution runs its own.

items.q: My child got a vmbo advice, what now?

blocks.p: vmbo takes 4 years and is a full route, not a dead end. After it comes mbo. The pathway matters: basis leads to mbo level 2, while kader, mixed or theoretical (gl/tl) lead to level 3 or 4. An mbo level 4 diploma gives the right to enter hbo, and from hbo wo is possible in most cases. That route takes more years than going straight through vwo, but every step exists.

ul: Ask which pathway the advice means: basis, kader or gl/tl.
Consider a school with several levels under one roof. A VO-raad factsheet argues that a broad first year keeps more options open. The school list shows this.
After vmbo gl/tl, moving to havo year 4 is possible with conditions. The school decides.
The advice is the school's judgement. The end-of-primary test can raise it, and the school must explain if it keeps a lower one.

items.q: Is repeating a year normal, and who decides?

blocks.p: The school decides whether a child moves up or repeats a year. There are no legal rules for it. The school guide describes how each school handles it. The school must tell you if your child repeats a year. If you disagree, you can object through the school's complaints procedure.

ul: Ask for the reasons in writing: which results and observations, and which support has been tried.
Ask for a meeting with the teacher and the school's learning-support coordinator (intern begeleider).
Repeating is not automatically good or bad. Ask the school what it expects to change.
If language is the issue, ask what support exists. Repeating a year may not fix a speech or pronunciation question, so ask the school and, if needed, a speech therapist.

blocks.p: We have no official figure for how common it is, so we do not give one.

items.q: How do I ask the school about the advice, or ask for a second opinion?

blocks.p: The school advice is the school's professional judgement of your child's whole record. The end-of-primary test can raise it, and the school must explain if it does not raise it. Secondary schools admit on the final advice, and they may not ask a primary school to give an advice for one level only.

blocks.say: Could we meet to talk about the advice? Which results and observations is it based on? What would change it?

ul: Ask for the final advice and the reasons in writing.
Ask whether the learning-support coordinator can join the meeting.
Independent assessments exist, for example from a child psychologist or an assessment bureau. Costs and insurance cover vary a lot, so ask before you book.
The advice is only advice for the child's next school. Ask the secondary schools you like what they need to admit your child.

items.q: Do I need an international school?

blocks.p: Not necessarily. Many families, including expat families, use Dutch schools. Some Dutch schools teach part of the lessons in English, such as international departments in primary school and bilingual Dutch-English (tto) streams in secondary school. A newcomer class helps children who are still learning Dutch.

International schools are mostly private, and fees vary widely. Parents report anything from a few thousand to well over twenty thousand euro a year. Those are reports, not checked figures, so ask each school. SIO lists international schools.
Think about how long you will stay, your child's age and the language your child will need later.

items.q: Is there a lottery for secondary school places?

blocks.p: Where a school has more applicants than places, a lottery can be used. It is not how most of the country works, as far as we know. Amsterdam runs a central lottery and matching procedure for secondary school. Some schools also select, for example on a test or an essay. Check your region and ask your child's school.

check.title: Check with the school and your municipality
check.text: Last checked: {date}. This page was written with AI assistance and each fact was compared with the official pages listed here. It has not yet been reviewed by a Dutch teacher or school advisor. Where sources differ, the page says "usually" or "most schools". Rules and dates change every year.

read.title: How to read the numbers
items: DUO, the Dutch education agency, hides any count below 5 pupils to protect privacy. When you see "fewer than 5", "at least" or "partial", some small groups are missing, so the real figure is a little higher.

The numbers are context for a conversation with a school, not a ranking. A high exam pass rate or a particular school advice mix also reflects which pupils the school admits. We never sort or colour schools by quality.

An Inspectie judgement is only published after a school visit, and visits are often triggered by concerns. Having a judgement, or not having one, says little by itself. The main judgement is the lowest of the programme judgements.
